infinity, \cite[Theorem~4.13 and Proposition~4.16]{BMPS26} constructs the
positive mixed operator
\[
 \MA_{\mathrm{poly}}:
 \mathrm{PC}_{\mathrm{reg}}(\mathbf X,\gamma)^d
 \longrightarrow\mathcal M^+(\mathbf X),
 \qquad
 \int_{\mathbf X}\MA_{\mathrm{poly}}=\deg(\gamma),
\]
and proves its continuity under uniform, in particular decreasing,
regularizable approximation.  Its Theorem~6.4 says that regularity is
equivalent to each of
\[
 \begin{split}
 &P_\gamma(u)\in\mathrm{PC}_{\mathrm{reg}}(\mathbf X,\gamma)
       \quad\text{for every bounded piecewise-affine }u,\\
 &\mathrm{PAPC}(\mathbf X,\gamma)
       \text{ is uniformly dense in }\mathrm{PC}(\mathbf X,\gamma),\\
 &\mathrm{PC}(\mathbf X,\gamma)
       =\mathrm{PC}_{\mathrm{reg}}(\mathbf X,\gamma).
 \end{split}
\]
The source states one-dimensional regularity in Proposition~6.13 and
complete-affine and conical regularization in Remark~6.6.  These statements
must be separated from its literal coefficient convention: Definition~2.28
requires integral linear parts and rational constants, while the proofs of
the cited regularization statements use arbitrary real affine functions.
The theorem and counterexample below give the precise one-dimensional
repair.  Orthogonality is the further
identity
\begin{equation}
 \int_{\mathbf X}
 \bigl(P_\gamma(u)-(\gamma+u)\bigr)
 \MA_{\mathrm{poly}}(P_\gamma(u))=0.
 \label{eq:frontier-polyhedral-orthogonality}
\end{equation}
The source proves \eqref{eq:frontier-polyhedral-orthogonality} on
one-dimensional polyhedrally smooth spaces and obtains existence and
uniqueness, modulo constants, for compactly supported positive measures of
mass \(\deg(\gamma)\)
\cite[Proposition~6.21 and Theorem~6.22]{BMPS26}.


This completely classifies the repaired real-piecewise-affine version of
P05.2 on every one-dimensional balanced rational polyhedral space admitting
a finite structure.  Orthogonality holds exactly when every local cone of
nonnegative balancing relations is one-dimensional.  The theorem allows
bounded edges and cycles and shows that lattice saturation is irrelevant.
In the literal coefficient category, one-dimensional regularity holds
exactly in degree zero, equivalently exactly when the space is compact.
Every positive-degree graph reference fails literal regularity,
independently of the local relation cones.  More generally, literal
regularity fails on every noncompact finite rational polyhedral space in
every dimension, whether or not it is balanced; in particular, the
source's literal complete-affine assertion fails in every positive
dimension.  The earlier strict-vertex theorem remains a local quantitative
form of this obstruction.  Thus every graph on which real-polyhedral
orthogonality holds is negative for literal regularity when the literal
degree is positive, but the literal failure is not confined to that graph
class.  The
one-vertex orthogonality theorem and its bounded-reference-shift corollary

note.  The classification also explains

smoothness is sufficient but not necessary in this class.  The

literal case, arbitrary nonseparable product obstacles, and the source

Its full top divisor is zero. Let \(T_j\) be the union of quotient fan faces of codimension at least \(j\). The first divisor vanishes off the preimage of \(T_1\), since the function is ambient affine there. Inductively, near the relative interior of a quotient face of codimension \(j-1\), the preceding cycle is supported in that face's preimage, where the function is affine on the entire supporting subspace. Extend this affine function to the ambient space; balancing makes its next divisor zero. Thus the \(j\)-th divisor is supported in the preimage of \(T_j\). Since \(T_{q+1}\) is empty, the top divisor vanishes. Rational common refinements and the local formula (5) justify this argument on every lower face, without transversality or a top-face-only measure formula.

## Exact triangle and comparison to residual scope

For \(A=(0,0)\), \(B=(1,0)\), \(C=(0,1)\), the oriented bounded primitive directions are \(a=(1,0)\), \(b=(-1,1)\), \(c=(0,-1)\), all of primitive length one. The leaves \(c-a=(-1,-1)\), \(a-b=(2,-1)\), \(b-c=(-1,2)\) are primitive. At each vertex the three outgoing vectors sum to zero and have rank two. Their only relation is the strictly positive unit vector. Their local lattice spans are saturated: each star contains a pair of determinant \(\pm1\). Thus this graph meets (1) with the actual lattices, and the theorem applies to \(G\times E\) in every dimension.

The tree amalgamation failure is still genuine as a diagnostic: before imposing the cycle period, \(a,b,c\) are independent and the formal walk ends at \(a+b+c\ne0\); closing the actual graph imposes \(a+b+c=0\). The incidence system (11) retains all three bounded edges and never uses that invalid lift. Its local contact proof also never groups remote generators into independent branches.

The controlling book already includes cycles in dimension one. Repeating that theorem is not the contribution. The result here is the full finite-graph-cylinder subclass in every affine dimension, all positive-growth real-PA PC references and bounded real-PA obstacles on finite rational spatial domains, including nonseparable functions. It addresses the concrete implementation assignment, while original P05.2's arbitrary balanced-space characterization remains open. The tree draft, prior two-vertex proof, and finite-dual proposal are not assumed correct. No additional smoothness hypothesis, separability hypothesis, regularity-failure alternative, or isolated negative-atom diagnostic substitutes for the exact contact theorem.

## Actual nonseparable cyclic example and exhaustive finite recursion

On the specified triangle times \(\mathbb R_z\), choose
\[
 \gamma(x,y,z)=\frac{|x|+|y|}{10}+|z|.
\]
This is the restriction of an ambient convex function and hence satisfies every actual PCC. Its end slopes in the graph direction are \(1/5,3/10,3/10\), and its vertical slopes are positive after the \(|z|\) subdivision; thus it is positive at infinity, including mixed recession directions. On each of the three A-incident edges let \(t\) be primitive distance from \(A\), and put
\[
 u(t,z)=-\frac32\max\{0,1-|z-1|-2t\};
\]
put \(u=0\) on the other edges. On the bounded A-incident edges \(t=1\) at their opposite endpoints, where the formula vanishes, so the function is globally continuous. All walls and endpoints are rational, and \(-3/2\leq u\leq0\). It is nonseparable: its values at \((t,z)=(0,1),(1/2,1),(0,0),(1/2,0)\) have nonzero rectangular difference.

Insert \(D,H,J\) at distance \(1/2\) from \(A\) along \(AB,AC\), and A's leaf, respectively. The dual domain is \([-1,1]\). For \(0\leq t\leq1/2\) on an A-incident edge with graph reference slope \(s\in\{1/10,1/10,1/5\}\), fibre vertices occur at \(z=0,2t,1,2-2t\). Comparing their values of \(f-pz\), for \(-1\leq p\leq1\), gives
\[
 F_p(t)=\min\{st,(s+3)t-\tfrac12-p\}.
\]
The candidates at \(2t\) and \(2-2t\) are no smaller than \(st\). For \(t\geq1/2\), \(u=0\), so the infimum is the graph reference value. Consequently the node caps are
\[
 F_p(A)=\min(0,-\tfrac12-p),\quad F_p(B)=F_p(C)=\tfrac1{10},\quad
 F_p(D)=F_p(H)=\tfrac1{20},\quad F_p(J)=\tfrac1{10}.
\]
The greatest feasible values of the complete six-node cyclic system are
\[
\begin{split}
 a_A&=\min(0,-\tfrac12-p),\\
 a_B=a_C&=\min(\tfrac1{10},-\tfrac15-p),\\
 a_D=a_H&=\min(\tfrac1{20},-\tfrac15-\tfrac p2,-\tfrac7{20}-p),\\
 a_J&=\min(\tfrac1{10},-\tfrac25-p).
\end{split}                                                       \tag{27}
\]
Here is a direct greatest-assignment check, not just an LP execution. For every feasible vector, bivalent inequalities give \(a_D\leq(a_A+a_B)/2\), \(a_H\leq(a_A+a_C)/2\), and \(a_J\leq a_A+1/10\). The B and C inequalities and those bounds imply \(2a_B-a_C\leq a_A+3/10\), \(2a_C-a_B\leq a_A+3/10\). Substitution yields \(a_B,a_C\leq a_A+3/10\); combine with their caps and A's cap, then bound D,H,J. These are exactly the coordinate upper bounds in (27). The displayed vector attains all those bounds simultaneously. Directly, its Laplacian slacks at A,B,C are respectively \((2/5,1/5,1/5)\) for \(p\leq-1/2\), \((7/5+2p,-3/10-p,-3/10-p)\) for \(-1/2\leq p\leq-3/10\), and \((4/5,0,0)\) for \(p\geq-3/10\); all other slacks are zero. Caps and feasibility follow. This proves maximality for every \(p\), including the entire cycle.

Use the exact formula (13), interpolating (27) on all six bounded intervals and the fixed slopes on the three tails. The common dual vertices are
\[
                         -1,\ -\tfrac12,\ -\tfrac3{10},\ 1.
\]
This is an explicit finite formula for the actual envelope by the theorem proved above. It is itself nonseparable: \(P(D,0)-P(A,0)=1/20\), whereas \(P(D,1)-P(A,1)=3/20\).

## Reproducibility and verification limits

`diagnostics.py` and `diagnostic-input.json` provide exact rational checks of the triangle stars and a three-node cyclic incidence toy system; `diagnostic-output.json` records the output. The toy system is explicitly not asserted to be the partial infimum of an actual obstacle. It checks incidence arithmetic only. `cyclic-example.py` and `cyclic-example-output.json` provide the actual nonseparable example and full recursion just displayed. `P05.2-partial.tex` is a standalone rendering of this argument; `P05.2-partial.pdf` was compiled twice. `build-evidence.json`, `source-hashes.json`, `environment.txt`, `commands.txt`, `author-self-audit.md`, and `research-notes.md` record environment, source provenance, build checks, and limitations. Rerun `python3 diagnostics.py`, `python3 cyclic-example.py`, and `python3 build.py`; the last command renders the TeX and compiles the PDF twice.

No supervised heavy-compute facility was available in the exposed tools; none was needed or launched. All computation is small exact arithmetic or document compilation. Successful execution, source hashes, and compilation are not mathematical verification. The theorem is an unverified proof draft and requires independent mathematical review of the supplied argument.

The maximization domains of a finite affine maximum, including all their faces and removing duplicates, form a complex: intersections are equality faces of the respective maxima regions. Its faces are rational because these regions are rational polyhedra. At a graph node (16)--(17) have exactly the same fibre domain for each \(p_0\), independent of the neighboring interval, so the strip complexes glue. This gives a finite rational spatial complex for \(P\) on the actual carrier. Moreover (16) has vertices only at its two graph endpoints, and (17) only at its base; faces introduce no new vertices. Thus every possible zero-dimensional domain face of this complex lies over a node of \(V\). Edge interiors cannot carry a recursive zero-cycle coefficient. This conclusion includes all bounded-edge interiors and all tails, rather than omitting their lower-face terms.

## PAPC against all local real cycles and actual regularization

Let \(z\geq0\) be any local real balanced cycle of any positive dimension on an ordinary open \(U\subset X\), and refine to make \(P\) affine. At a tested facet \(\tau\), choose a rational \(x\in U\cap\operatorname{relint}\tau\). The cone of possible nonnegative incident weights balanced modulo \(N_\tau\) is a rational polyhedral cone, so is generated by rational vectors, by the elementary cone proof above. The divisor coefficient is linear in those weights. It suffices to test a nonnegative rational incident vector \(c_\sigma\).

Write \(S=\sum c_\sigma>0\), \(B=\sum c_\sigma n_{\sigma/\tau}\in N_{\tau,\mathbb Q}\), and use the rational inward vectors \(n_{\sigma/\tau}-B/S\). They need not be integral normals; they have the same positive quotient directions. For sufficiently small rational \(\varepsilon>0\), the rational points \(x_\sigma=x+\varepsilon(n_{\sigma/\tau}-B/S)\) belong to \(\sigma\cap U\). With coefficients \(c_\sigma/S\) their barycentre is \(x\), giving an actual PCC. Its Jensen inequality is
\[

       =\varepsilon\left(\sum c_\sigma P_\sigma(n_{\sigma/\tau})-P_\tau(B)\right).
\]
This is exactly (5). The zero-weight case is zero. Rational-generation then proves the inequality for every nonnegative real incident vector, and hence for every real local cycle. Thus \(P\) is PAPC in the full required sense. Balancing proved above permits recursion, and every successive divisor is nonnegative. Its full top cycle is a finite nonnegative atomic measure on the rational domain vertices. The sequence \(P+1/j\) is PAPC in the same two-sided growth class and decreases uniformly to \(P\); its divisors agree with those of \(P\). This establishes the actual operator domain and regularization without invoking source regularity assertions.

## Two complete recursive vanishing lemmas

**Quotient vanishing.** On a local \(d\)-cycle, suppose that after subtracting an ambient affine function the PA germ is pulled back by a rational linear map to a function on a complete rational fan in a space of dimension \(q<d\). Its full top divisor is zero. Let \(T_j\) be the union of quotient fan faces of codimension at least \(j\). The first divisor vanishes off the preimage of \(T_1\), since the function is ambient affine there. Inductively, near the relative interior of a quotient face of codimension \(j-1\), the preceding cycle is supported in that face's preimage, where the function is affine on the entire supporting subspace. Extend this affine function to the ambient space; balancing makes its next divisor zero. Thus the \(j\)-th divisor is supported in the preimage of \(T_j\). Since \(T_{q+1}\) is empty, the top divisor vanishes. Rational common refinements and the local formula (5) justify this argument on every lower face, without transversality or a top-face-only measure formula.

**Lineality vanishing.** If the local carrier fan and residual function-domain fan have common nonzero rational lineality, choose their common generalized fan retaining that lineality. Every face contains it; there is no zero-dimensional face. Every recursive divisor lives on that fan, so the top zero-cycle is zero. Refinement cannot change this by the proved refinement identity. Ambient affine terms can be removed first.

Let $\mathbf X$ be a one-dimensional balanced rational polyhedral space,
and fix a finite rational polyhedral structure $\Pi$ carrying its balancing
cycle.  For a vertex $v\in\Pi^{(0)}$, write $E(v)$ for the incident edges,
$u_{e/v}$ for the primitive outgoing integral direction of $e$ at $v$, and
$w_e>0$ for the balancing weight of $e$.  Put
\[
 K_v:=\left\{\lambda\in\mathbf R_{\geq0}^{E(v)}:\
             \sum_{e\in E(v)}\lambda_eu_{e/v}=0\right\}.
\]
The local weight vector $w_v=(w_e)_{e\in E(v)}$ belongs to the relative
interior of $K_v$.

\begin{theorem}
\label{thm:frontier-polyhedral-local-rank-one-graph}
Assume that $\dim K_v=1$ for every vertex $v\in\Pi^{(0)}$.  Let
$\gamma\in\mathrm{PA}_{\mathbf R}(\mathbf X)\cap
\mathrm{PC}(\mathbf X)$ be positive at infinity.  Then
$(\mathbf X,\gamma)$ has real-polyhedral orthogonality: for every
$u\in\mathrm{PA}_{\mathbf R,b}(\mathbf X)$,
\[
 \int_{\mathbf X}
 \bigl(P_\gamma(u)-(\gamma+u)\bigr)
 \MA_{\mathrm{poly},\mathbf R}(P_\gamma(u))=0.
\]
The conclusion allows bounded edges and cycles in the underlying graph.
It depends only on the local cones $K_v$ and is unchanged by subdividing
$\Pi$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}
\label{cor:frontier-polyhedral-trivalent-graph}
Every one-dimensional balanced rational polyhedral space admitting a finite
structure whose vertices have valence at most three satisfies the conclusion
of \Cref{thm:frontier-polyhedral-local-rank-one-graph} for every
real-piecewise-affine polyhedrally convex reference positive at infinity.
In particular, lattice saturation and the absence of bounded cycles are not
required.
\end{corollary}

The theorem is a sufficient criterion, not a converse.  At a vertex with
$\dim K_v>1$, the one-vertex construction gives a local noncontact mass
mechanism, but extending that germ through all bounded edges while retaining
global polyhedral convexity and the prescribed growth is a separate
realizability problem.

\begin{proof}[\Cref{thm:frontier-polyhedral-local-rank-one-graph}]
Fix $u\in\mathrm{PA}_{\mathbf R,b}(\mathbf X)$, put
\[
 a:=\gamma+u,
 \qquad
 f:=P_\gamma(u),
 \qquad
 \mu:=\MA_{\mathrm{poly},\mathbf R}(f).
\]
After a common finite refinement, $a$ is real-piecewise affine.  The
real-affine proof of the one-dimensional envelope statement in
\cite[Proposition~6.13]{BMPS26} gives
$f\in\mathrm{PA}_{\mathbf R}(\mathbf X)\cap\mathrm{PC}(\mathbf X)$
on that refinement.  Consequently $\mu$ is a nonnegative atomic measure
supported at its vertices.  A newly inserted vertex in the interior of an
old edge has two opposite primitive directions and equal inherited weights,
so its cone of nonnegative balancing relations is one-dimensional.  Thus the
hypothesis persists under the refinement.

We show that every point carrying positive $\mu$-mass lies in the contact
set $\{f=a\}$.  Let $v$ be a vertex of the refined structure, let $s_e$ be
the outgoing slope of $f$ along $e\in E(v)$, and suppose
\[
 m:=\mu\{v\}=\sum_{e\in E(v)}w_es_e>0,
 \qquad
 f(v)<a(v).
\]
For every incident edge choose a point $x_e$ at integral-affine distance
$\rho_e>0$ from $v$, so close that the open segment $(v,x_e)$ contains no
other vertex and $f$ is affine on $[v,x_e]$.  The continuous function
$a-f$ is positive at $v$, hence is bounded below by a positive constant on
a sufficiently small closed star; choose the points inside that star.

For $\delta>0$, define $f_\delta$ by raising the value at $v$ from $f(v)$
to $f(v)+\delta$, interpolating affinely from that new value to the unchanged
value $f(x_e)$ on every segment $[v,x_e]$, and leaving $f$ unchanged
elsewhere.  Choose $\delta$ smaller than the obstacle gap and so small that
\[
 0<\delta<
 \frac{m}{\sum_{e\in E(v)}w_e/\rho_e}.
\]
The new outgoing slope at $v$ along $e$ is
$s_e-\delta/\rho_e$.  Since $K_v=\mathbf R_{\geq0}w_v$, the local
polyhedral-convexity inequalities at $v$ reduce to the single inequality
\[
 \sum_e w_e\left(s_e-\frac{\delta}{\rho_e}\right)
 =m-\delta\sum_e\frac{w_e}{\rho_e}>0.
\]
At $x_e$, the slope on the segment from $v$ has decreased by
$\delta/\rho_e$ in the coordinate pointing away from $v$ and then returns
to the old slope.  Ordinary one-variable convexity is therefore preserved.
All other local convexity inequalities are unchanged.  The local
one-dimensional slope criterion, equivalently
\cite[Definitions~3.1--3.3 and Lemma~3.4]{BMPS26}, now shows that
$f_\delta$ is polyhedrally convex.

Moreover $f_\delta\leq a$, and $f_\delta-f$ has compact support, so
$f_\delta\leq\gamma+O(1)$.  Hence $f_\delta$ is an admissible competitor
for $P_\gamma(u)$ and satisfies $f_\delta(v)>f(v)$, contradicting the
definition of the envelope.  We conclude that
\[
 \operatorname{supp}\mu\subseteq\{f=a\}.
\]
The integrand $f-a$ vanishes on the support of the nonnegative atomic
measure $\mu$, and the asserted orthogonality integral is therefore zero.
The argument is local at the vertices and never removes a bounded edge or
cuts a graph cycle, proving the last two assertions.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[\Cref{cor:frontier-polyhedral-trivalent-graph}]
Balancing excludes a one-valent vertex.  At a two-valent vertex the two
primitive outgoing directions are opposite, and its positive balancing
relation spans $K_v$.  At a three-valent vertex, the three distinct outgoing
rays cannot all lie in a one-dimensional vector subspace.  Their span
therefore has dimension two, and the kernel of the direction map
$\mathbf R^3\to N_{\mathbf R}$ is one-dimensional.  Its positive balancing
vector spans $K_v$.  Thus every vertex satisfies $\dim K_v=1$, and
\Cref{thm:frontier-polyhedral-local-rank-one-graph} applies.
\end{proof}
## Finite partial-infimum data, with tails and recession constraints

Work in one connected component, identify \(E\) rationally with its lattice vector space, and take a common finite rational affine structure for \(f=\gamma+u\) and \(\gamma\), refined by the original edge strips. Each cell is pointed: a nonzero lineality direction would give two opposite reference recession slopes, incompatible with positivity at infinity. Formula (4) therefore applies.

For each cell ray with zero graph coordinate, write its affine obstacle slope as \(s_r\) and its \(E\)-coordinate as \(r_E\), and define
\[
 D=\{p\in E^*:p(r_E)\leq s_r\text{ for every such ray}\}.                    \tag{8}
\]
All inequality normals are rational; constants may be real. On every recession ray \(u\) has zero slope, by boundedness, so (8) is the same for \(f\) and \(\gamma\). It contains 0 in its interior, because every nonzero vertical ray has strictly positive reference slope. For \(m=0\), \(D=\{0\}\) in the zero-dimensional dual space.

Set \(F_p(q)=\inf_{z\in E}(f(q,z)-p(z))\). For \(p\in D\) this is finite at every \(q\) and its infimum is attained at a vertex of some cell fibre. Indeed, the fibre is pointed and its recession cone is generated by the zero-graph cell rays: graph recession is zero on bounded strips and nonnegative on unbounded strips, so a zero-graph combination cannot use any positive-graph ray. The objective is nonnegative on this recession cone, and (4) for the fibre gives a minimizing vertex. There are finitely many cells. If \(p\notin D\), a violating rational ray based at a rational point gives \(F_p(q)=-\infty\) at a rational graph point. Thus (8) is precisely the common finite domain required here.

The set \(D\) is compact. At any fixed rational graph vertex, the finite-PA function \(f(q,z)\) is bounded above by \(M\|z\|+B\), for some finite \(M,B\) (use finitely many affine pieces and the dual norm). If \(\|p\|>M\), a direction with \(p(z)>M\|z\|\) makes the infimum \(-\infty\). Finiteness for \(p\in D\) bounds \(D\). This proof does not require \(f\) convex.

Subdivide each bounded edge at the graph coordinates of all its spatial cell vertices, and each end at those coordinates and its original base. This is finite and rational. Between consecutive coordinates a fibre vertex lies on a spatial one-face: the minimal face containing it loses one dimension under the slicing hyperplane, so has dimension at most one. A one-face traversing the interval has rational form \(z(t)=z_i+t b_i\), and obstacle height real-affine in \(t\). Its feasibility across that open interval is constant, because changes occur only at projected spatial vertices. Therefore on each such interval
\[
 F_p(t)=\min_i\{A_i(p)+t B_i(p)\},                      \tag{9}
\]
where the finite index set is independent of \(p\); \(A_i,B_i\) are affine in \(p\), with rational linear coefficients and real constants. At a node \(v\), slicing the cells directly gives \(F_p(v)\) as a finite minimum of affine functions of \(p\), again with rational gradients and real constants.

For clarity, (9) extends concavely and continuously to each finite interval endpoint. Its candidate fibre vertices have finite limits there, so their limiting objective values are at least \(F_p(v)\). Conversely, fixing any finite \(z\) and using continuity of \(f(t,z)\) gives \(\limsup_{t\to v}F_p(t)\leq f(v,z)-p(z)\); then take its infimum over \(z\). This proves equality of the limits. It also proves branchwise continuity at a graph vertex. The possibility of a different endpoint fibre type is not discarded.

After the last projected vertex on an end, translate its primitive parameter to start at 0. Formula (9) holds for all \(t\geq0\), and
\[
 \theta_e(p):=\lim_{t\to\infty}F_p(t)/t=\min_i B_i(p),\qquad

Let \(V\) be the finite node set just obtained. For fixed \(p\in D\), introduce node values \(a_v\), and impose
\[

The componentwise maximum of two feasible assignments is feasible. At a node attaining its value from one assignment, each neighboring value has only increased, so \(L_v\) has not decreased; the caps also persist. Choose a feasible witness \(b\). Maximizing \(\sum_v a_v\) after taking componentwise maximum with \(b\) restricts to the compact box \(b_v\leq a_v\leq F_p(v)\), and hence attains a maximum. \section{Detailed regularity and descent results}
\label{sec:appM-regularity-results}

Classical pluriharmonicity is defined by curve tests after arbitrary ground
field extension and therefore does not visibly provide a finite local
presentation by logarithms of analytic units.  On the quasi-smooth locus,
altered local uniformization and rigid $\acute{e}$tale descent remove this
gap.  The descent step is included because the uniformizing cover need not be
finite, flat, or boundaryless, so finite-flat descent cannot be applied to it
directly.

\begin{corollary}[Finite-flat cover descent for classical pluriharmonic regularity]
\label{cor:p061-finite-flat-cover-descent}
Let $K$ be a complete nontrivially valued field and let
$\pi:Y\to X$ be a finite, flat, surjective morphism of good strictly
$K$-analytic spaces.  Suppose that every classically pluriharmonic
function on every ordinary open subspace of $Y$ is $\mathbf R$-PL.
Then every classically pluriharmonic function on every ordinary open subspace
of $X$ is $\mathbf R$-PL and Gubler--Jell--Rabinoff harmonic.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Let $U$ be an ordinary open subspace of $X$, let
$h\in\operatorname{PH}(U)$, and fix $x\in U$.  Choose a good strict
affinoid neighbourhood $U_0\subseteq U$ of $x$.  The restricted map
\[
 \pi^{-1}(U_0)\longrightarrow U_0
\]
is finite, flat, and surjective between good strictly $K$-analytic
spaces.  Classical pluriharmonicity is stable under analytic pullback
\cite[Proposition~7.2(6)]{GR25Classical}, so $\pi^*h$ is
$\mathbf R$-PL on $\pi^{-1}(U_0)$ by hypothesis.  Apply
\cite[Proposition~5.11]{GJR26} with the divisible coefficient group
$\Lambda=\mathbf R$.  It descends $\mathbf R$-PL regularity to
$h|_{U_0}$.  Since $x$ was arbitrary, $h$ is $\mathbf R$-PL on
$U$.

Both $h$ and $-h$ are classically psh.  The real-PL comparison
\cite[Theorem~4.3]{GR25Classical} makes both signs semipositive, which is
exactly Gubler--Jell--Rabinoff harmonicity.
\end{proof}
